about: What each scenario tests. Read only when analysing results: never shown to the agent under test or to the judges.

kinds.rule-out: A constraint rules out the obvious or first-proposed choice.
kinds.stay: The team's existing stack is right; a good answer does not push a rewrite.
kinds.gap: lang-bench's data does not cover what decides this; a good answer says what to measure.
kinds.not-performance: Performance barely matters; team, maintenance and cost decide.

01-studio-booking.tests: Whether the agent picks something a non-technical owner can live with (hosted, low upkeep) rather than an interesting stack.

02-discord-stats.covered: Idle memory per stack at 512 MB.
02-discord-stats.tests: Python fits; the student's learning goal and the memory limit are the only constraints.

03-webhook-fanout.covered: I/O-wait workload: Node async servers hold thousands of waits per core.
03-webhook-fanout.tests: Node is fine for I/O-bound fan-out; a rewrite in Go is not needed. Queues and retries matter more.

04-pdf-reports.covered: CPU workload: a single event loop blocks other requests while computing.
04-pdf-reports.tests: CPU work inside the Express event loop is ruled out; moving it to workers or a job queue fixes it, with or without a new language.

05-tv-campaign.covered: Laravel on PHP-FPM serves a few hundred requests per second per core; Octane about twice that.
05-tv-campaign.tests: Plain PHP-FPM on 2 vCPUs can't take 3,000 req/s; caching, a CDN, Octane or more servers fix it without a rewrite.

06-webhook-delivery-rails.covered: I/O-wait workload: thread-per-request servers hold as many waits as threads.
06-webhook-delivery-rails.tests: Threads per Sidekiq process cap concurrent slow POSTs; more concurrency (threads, async HTTP, more processes) or a Go service both work. A good answer weighs the Go team's capacity against fixing it in Ruby.

08-payment-status-api.covered: Spring Boot handles 800 req/s on a database read comfortably per core.
08-payment-status-api.tests: Spring Boot meets the requirement; Go would break the approved-technology list for no gain.

09-partner-callbacks.covered: I/O-wait workload: java-spring (200 platform threads) against java-spring-vt (virtual threads).
09-partner-callbacks.tests: Platform threads are ruled out at 10,000 waiting connections; virtual threads or a reactive stack fix it within Java.

10-order-notifications.covered: Start-up time per runtime in containers, though not on Azure Functions.
10-order-notifications.tests: .NET meets a 2 s budget with cold starts, especially with ready-to-run or a premium plan; a rewrite isn't needed. Partly a gap: serverless cold starts aren't measured.

11-simulation-service.covered: Nothing: the work is NumPy, not request handling.
11-simulation-service.tests: The web framework doesn't matter; a job queue in Python does. A good answer doesn't send them to learn a new language.

12-variant-search.covered: Nothing about large in-memory indexes or Python lookup cost.
12-variant-search.tests: Whether the agent recommends measuring a lookup first (loaded once, served by workers sharing memory) before a C++ rewrite.

13-gateway-api.covered: Idle memory and start-up per stack, on x86-64 only.
13-gateway-api.tests: JVM and most interpreted stacks are ruled out by 20 MB and 1 s; Rust or C++ fit the team. ARM isn't measured.

14-volunteer-rota.tests: A mainstream, easily hired stack, or an off-the-shelf rota product, beats anything niche; data protection matters.

15-matchmaking.covered: Nothing on WebSockets or long-lived connections.
15-matchmaking.tests: Node can hold 50,000 sockets across a few processes; Elixir is a reasonable alternative but a team change. A good answer says what to load-test.

16-friend-recommendations.tests: Whether the agent weighs Postgres recursive queries and precomputation against adding a graph database, and says the language matters little.
